epic.name: Sign in and the signed-in app shell
unverifiedAssumptions: Verify the role names the service actually returns for your two accounts: the app decides what you are offered by matching your account's role to exactly "Finance Uploader" or "Approver". The sign-in service's own documentation shows a different example role ("Viewer"), and the source material flags that naming inconsistency. If the real names differ in wording or spelling, a signed-in user could be offered nothing at all, or be offered actions that are not theirs.

Verify how the sign-in service handles time and repeated failures: the app assumes that staying active keeps your session alive, warns you about a minute before it would drop you, and assumes the service itself reports a temporarily locked account after repeated wrong passwords. If the service uses a different session length, does not extend it while you work, or does not track failed attempts, you may be signed out with no warning, or never see a lockout message — the app cannot count attempts or hold a session open on its own.

Verify one real sign-in in a browser, end to end: the app is built so the browser only ever calls the app's own address, which forwards on to the two backend services — that is what sidesteps the cross-origin permission header neither service currently returns. If any call reaches a service directly, sign-in will fail in the browser with nothing on screen to explain why, even though every automated test passes.

When the auth service is unreachable or returns a 500, a signed-in person sees an error rather than being returned to the sign-in screen. Only an expired/rejected session sends them to sign-in. Confirm that is the behaviour you want when a backend is down.

The /transactions-api/* forwarding rule is set up but nothing in this epic calls the transactions service, so the forwarded address shape is unverified against the live service. The first story that reads transaction data will prove it.
The session cookie is treated as Secure everywhere except when BFF_INSECURE_COOKIE=1 is set for local plain-HTTP development. Confirm the deployed environments are HTTPS.

Wording for the two sign-in failures the API contract doesn't specify: a refusal with no explanation from the service shows 'Sign-in failed. Check your details and try again.', and an unreachable/broken auth service shows 'Sign-in is unavailable right now. Please try again in a moment.' Confirm both read the way you want them to.

The sign-in screen's copy: heading 'Sign in', helper line 'Sign in with your username and password to reach the expense screens.', required-field legend '* indicates a required field', and the button label 'Sign in'. No prototype or design source specified this screen's copy.

A successful sign-in always lands on / (the app's main signed-in screen). There is no 'return to where you were trying to go' behaviour yet — if a bookmarked deep link should be honoured after signing in, that's a change to make.

Identity is presented as the person's full name with their role beneath it, inside a header menu button, and Sign out lives in that menu rather than as a standalone header button. The requirement only says 'display the signed-in user's identity' (R3) — confirm this is the shape you want, since the theme switch sits beside it.
The header's app name reads 'Employee Expenses' and the landing screen's heading/intro wording was written during the build — no source document specifies either.
